name: Ownership
definition: Leaders are owners. They think long-term and don't sacrifice long-term value for short-term results. They act on behalf of the entire company, beyond just their own team, and never compromise safety. They never say, "that's not my job."

rows.situation: When the work sits outside your job description
rows.under: Says it is not their job and walks past it.
rows.justRight: Picks it up, or stays until a real owner has it. Never leaves it sitting.
rows.over: Takes over work that already has an owner so they can be the hero.

rows.situation: When the right call hurts your team and helps the company
rows.justRight: Makes the call for the whole company and explains the cost to your team.
rows.over: Gives away your team's commitments so often that they cannot deliver what they own.

rows.situation: When a short-term result would cost next year
rows.under: Takes the short-term win and leaves the bill for later.
rows.justRight: Protects the long-term value, including when it makes this month look worse.
rows.over: Invokes the long term to avoid a result that is actually due now.

rows.situation: When a shortcut would touch safety
rows.under: Treats safety as someone else's checklist.
rows.justRight: Will not trade safety for schedule, cost, or convenience. Escalates until the risk is real and owned.
rows.over: Stops all progress in the name of safety without naming the actual risk.

rows.situation: When a problem has no owner
rows.justRight: Takes it far enough that it has an owner and a next step.
rows.over: Collects unowned work until nothing they already owned can finish.

rows.situation: When you raised a problem outside your area
rows.under: Flags it once and lets go.
rows.justRight: Stays until a capable owner is on it and the fix is in motion.
rows.over: Hovers over the other team after they have taken it, and becomes the bottleneck.
